assessment.Interference with freedom of expression: The applicant’s conduct fell within Article 10. He wore a transparent visor bearing the words “smash capitalism” during a protest linked to the opening of the ECB headquarters, plainly a political event and a matter of public interest (see paragraphs 5-6). His subsequent criminal conviction and fine for wearing that visor at the demonstration constituted an interference with his freedom of expression, because the sanction targeted the manner in which he chose to convey his political message (see paragraphs 8-12). Even though the final penalty was reduced to 10 daily rates, a criminal conviction in the context of political protest is capable of producing a chilling effect. Political expression enjoys strong protection and the State’s margin of appreciation is correspondingly narrow (see nos. 20652/92, 8029/07).

assessment.Lawfulness and legitimate aim: The interference had a basis in domestic law, namely sections 17a(1) and 27(1) of the Act on Public Assemblies and Processions (see paragraphs 17-18), and it can plausibly be said to have pursued legitimate aims such as the prevention of disorder or crime and the protection of public safety, especially given the serious violence surrounding the ECB protests on the same day (see paragraph 7). The critical issue, however, is whether the interference was “prescribed by law” in the Convention sense, including foreseeability. The legislative materials defined “protective weapons” as objects usually given a defensive purpose at the time of manufacture, giving examples such as protective shields, self-made armour, steel helmets, gas masks and martial-arts equipment; they also stressed that mere symbolic use for expressing an opinion should not fall within the prohibition (see paragraph 19).

assessment.Foreseeability of the criminal prohibiti: On the facts, the applicant wore a relatively simple piece of transparent plastic sheeting held by a rubber band, on which he had written a slogan (see paragraph 6). The police present at the demonstration neither warned him, nor ordered him to remove it, nor fined him on the spot (see paragraph 6). Yet the domestic courts treated the visor as a “protective weapon” through a notably expansive and inconsistent interpretation. The District Court relied on the idea that no “civil” use was imaginable and that it could protect against pepper spray (see paragraph 10). The Regional Court went further and stated that its defensive purpose had been assigned at the time of manufacture “as follows from the inscription ‘smash capitalism’” (see paragraph 13), although that inscription was evidently added by the applicant and was part of the expressive element. In a criminal-law context, such reasoning appears strained and insufficiently foreseeable. It is difficult to conclude that an ordinary participant in a political demonstration could reasonably predict that this homemade, slogan-bearing visor would be treated like the kinds of defensive equipment listed in the legislative history. This points to a lack of the required quality of law and an excessive scope for arbitrary application (see nos. 37101/97, 30582/04, 15367/14).

assessment.Insufficient regard to the expressive el: The domestic courts also failed to engage convincingly with the expressive aspect of the applicant’s conduct. They accepted that the visor bore a political slogan, but dismissed that element on the basis that he could have worn it on the back of his head instead (see paragraph 11). That response did not genuinely balance the applicant’s interest in expressing himself, in the form he chose, against the public-order concerns relied on by the authorities. Given the high level of protection afforded to political speech, such a cursory treatment reinforces the conclusion that the interference was not Convention-compliant (see nos. 8080/08, 68537/13).

assessment.Overall conclusion: Although the State could legitimately seek to prevent disorder at a tense and partially violent protest, the applicant’s conviction appears to rest on an unforeseeable extension of the criminal prohibition on “protective weapons” to a homemade visor carrying a political message (see paragraphs 6, 10, 13 and 19). Because the interference was likely not “prescribed by law” for the purposes of Article 10 § 2, the Court would likely find a violation of Article 10.
